# Release signing keys

Everything a maintainer, the release pipeline and a user need in order to produce and check a
signed rspinyin release. Nothing in this directory is secret: the private half of the key
lives in the repository's CI secrets and nowhere else.

## The rule that is not negotiable

**No private key, passphrase or token is ever committed, and none is ever generated by an
automated step.** The private key is created by the maintainer on their own machine, stored as
the repository secret `RSPINYIN_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY`, and deleted from every machine it was ever
exported to. Only the armored public key -- `rspinyin-signing-key.asc`, in this directory -- is
committed, because a user has to be able to import it without a keyserver.

If a private key is ever committed by accident, the key is compromised. Deleting the commit is
not enough: rotate the key, publish the new public half, and say so in the release notes.

## Files here

| File | What it is | Committed |
|---|---|---|
| `rspinyin-signing-key.asc` | The armored public key users import to check a release | yes |
| `README.md` | This file | yes |

`rspinyin-signing-key.asc` is not in the repository yet. It appears the first time a
maintainer runs the procedure below; until then `release.yml` fails on its first step, which is
the intended behaviour rather than a gap -- a release pipeline with no key to sign with must
not be able to produce an unsigned release and call it done.

## Placeholders used below

The commands are written with these placeholders rather than with real values, because the
values are the key's identity and cannot be known before it exists:

| Placeholder | Where it comes from | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|
| `<FINGERPRINT>` | `gpg --list-secret-keys --with-colons` prints it as the `fpr` record | the repository secret `RSPINYIN_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` holds the *key*; the pipeline reads the fingerprint out of the imported key itself rather than storing it a second time |
| `<KEY_ID>` | the last 16 hexadecimal digits of `<FINGERPRINT>` | `gpg --local-user <KEY_ID>` when signing by hand |

Do not write either value into a committed file. A manifest records the fingerprint of the key
that signed it, but the manifest is a build product under `dist/`, not a source file.

## Creating the key (maintainer, once)

```bash
# 1. Generate the key. Ed25519 is the modern default; RSA 4096 is the interoperable
#    alternative if a distribution's tooling is old enough to matter.
gpg --full-generate-key

# 2. Find its fingerprint. The `fpr` line under the `sec` line is the fingerprint.
gpg --list-secret-keys --with-colons | awk -F: '$1 == "fpr" { print $10 }'

# 3. Export the public half into the repository and commit it.
gpg --armor --export <FINGERPRINT> > packaging/keys/rspinyin-signing-key.asc
git add packaging/keys/rspinyin-signing-key.asc

# 4. Export the private half and store it as the repository secret
#    RSPINYIN_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY. Then delete the export.
gpg --armor --export-secret-keys <FINGERPRINT> > /tmp/rspinyin-private.asc
gh secret set RSPINYIN_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY < /tmp/rspinyin-private.asc
shred --remove /tmp/rspinyin-private.asc

# 5. Assert the export is gone before doing anything else.
test ! -e /tmp/rspinyin-private.asc && echo "no local copy of the private key"
```

The key must have no passphrase for the pipeline to use it unattended. That is a real tradeoff
and it is made deliberately: the secret is readable by anyone who can run a workflow in this
repository, so the trust boundary is the repository's own permissions. Set them accordingly,
and keep the key's expiry short enough that a leaked secret stops being useful.

## Signing (the release pipeline)

`.github/workflows/release.yml` does all of this. It is written out here so that a maintainer
can reproduce a release by hand, and so that the ordering -- which is the part that is easy to
get wrong -- is documented in one place.

```bash
# 1. Build and package. The manifest is written with "signature": null at this point, because
#    a placeholder key id would read like a signature that had been checked.
just package

# 2. Record the signing key in the manifest. This happens *before* the checksum list, because
#    the list covers the manifest: a manifest edited afterwards would no longer be covered by
#    the signature.
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, pathlib
path = pathlib.Path("dist/rspinyin-release.json")
document = json.loads(path.read_text())
document["signature"] = {
    "scheme": "openpgp",
    "key_id": "<FINGERPRINT>",
    "detached": "SHA256SUMS.asc",
}
path.write_text(json.dumps(document, indent=2) + "\n")
PY

# 3. Regenerate the checksum list over everything in dist/ except the list itself and the
#    signature over it. `xtask verify` requires exactly this coverage.
cd dist
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f ! -name 'SHA256SUMS' ! -name 'SHA256SUMS.asc' -printf '%P\n' \
  | sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS

# 4. Sign the list, and check the signature immediately.
gpg --batch --yes --local-user <FINGERPRINT> \
    --detach-sign --armor --output SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS
gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS
```

## Verifying (a user)

No keyserver is involved at any point, and none may be: the public key ships with the release,
and a verification that fetched a key would be a network operation inside a product that
promises never to open a socket.

```bash
# 1. Import the key that came with the release.
gpg --import packaging/keys/rspinyin-signing-key.asc

# 2. Check the signature over the checksum list.
gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS

# 3. Check the checksum list, and then the release's own records.
sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS
cargo run --quiet -p xtask -- verify \
    --manifest rspinyin-release.json \
    --artifacts .
```

`xtask verify` reads only. It does not install, replace or remove anything, and it never looks
for a newer release: there is no update channel, and upgrades arrive through the distribution's
package manager. It reports a verdict and an exit status, and on failure it prints one of the
`dist/*` codes from the delivery contract in `docs/dev/opt-deploy.md` section 3.3.2.

The codes a user is most likely to meet, and what each one means for them:

| Code | What to do |
|---|---|
| `dist/verify/signing-key-absent` | Import `packaging/keys/rspinyin-signing-key.asc`; the key that signed this release is not in your keyring |
| `dist/verify/signature-invalid` | Do not install the release. Re-download it from the original source; if it fails again, report it |
| `dist/verify/digest-mismatch` | The bytes do not match the records. Do not install; re-download |
| `dist/verify/artifact-missing` | A file the records name is not in the directory. The download is incomplete |
| `dist/verify/factory-symbol-missing` | The library would load without an addon. Do not install |
| `dist/verify/dictionary-invalid` | The dictionary failed its own format and checksum checks. Do not install |
| `dist/verify/size-budget-exceeded` | A file is past the ceiling the manifest records. Do not install |
| `dist/manifest/*` | The manifest is unreadable or from a newer release; check you have the matching version of `xtask` |

An expired or revoked key is refused as `dist/verify/signature-invalid` rather than accepted
with a warning. That refusal is deliberate: it is the only moment at which the user can be told
that the key they trust has stopped being trustworthy.

## Rotating the key

1. Generate the replacement and commit the new public half as described above.
2. Store the new private half in `RSPINYIN_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY`, replacing the old value.
3. Sign the next release with the new key. The manifest records which key signed it, so a user
   with both public keys can check either release without being told which is which.
4. Publish the rotation in the release notes, with the new fingerprint, and revoke the old key
   if it is suspected of being compromised.

Do not re-sign an already published release with a new key: the manifest and the checksum list
are covered by the signature, so a re-signed release is a different release.
